title: Memory Management & Performance
description: Master memory pooling, stack allocation with Span<T>, ref structs, and avoid common GC pressure issues.

data.text: .NET uses a generational garbage collector with three generations (0, 1, 2). Understanding how objects are allocated and collected is essential for writing high-performance code, especially in high-throughput scenarios.

data.caption: Generational GC flow
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[New object] --> B[Gen 0]
    B -->|Survives collection| C[Gen 1]
    C -->|Survives collection| D[Gen 2]
    D -->|Survives collection| D
    B -->|Collected| E[Freed]
    C -->|Collected| E
    D -->|Collected| E
    F[Large object heap] -->|LOH collection| E

data.title: GC Generations Explained
data.text: Gen 0: Short-lived objects, collected frequently. Gen 1: Buffer between short-lived and long-lived. Gen 2: Long-lived objects, collected infrequently. LOH: Objects > 85KB, collected with Gen 2.

Value types (struct, int, bool, etc.) are allocated on the stack when local variables. Reference types (class, string, etc.) are allocated on the heap. Stack allocation is faster and doesn't pressure the GC.

data.title: Value Types vs Reference Types

data.text: Span<T> provides a safe view into contiguous memory without allocation. It enables stack-based operations on arrays, stackalloc memory, and other memory regions. This is critical for parsing, string manipulation, and high-performance scenarios.

data.title: Span<T> for Zero-Allocation Parsing
Ref Structs
data.text: Span<T> is a ref struct, meaning it can only live on the stack. It cannot be boxed, stored in fields of classes, or used in async methods. These restrictions ensure it cannot escape the stack frame.
ArrayPool<T> rents arrays from a shared pool, reducing allocations for temporary buffers. Instead of allocating new arrays repeatedly, rent from the pool and return when done.

data.title: ArrayPool<T> for Buffer Reuse

data.text: For custom memory pools or unmanaged memory, use MemoryPool<T> and IMemoryOwner<T>. This pattern is especially useful when working with native libraries or custom allocation strategies.

data.title: Custom Memory Pool

cards.title: Boxing
cards.description: Converting value types to object causes heap allocation. Use generics or avoid boxing.

cards.title: String Concatenation in Loops
cards.description: Using + in loops creates many intermediate strings. Use StringBuilder instead.

cards.title: Closure Capture
cards.description: Capturing variables in closures allocates closure classes. Be aware of what you capture.

cards.title: LINQ in Hot Paths
cards.description: LINQ allocates iterators and delegates. In performance-critical code, use loops.

data.title: Avoiding Common Pitfalls

data.text: Use diagnostic tools to identify memory issues: dotnet-counters for real-time metrics, dotnet-dump for crash dumps, and Visual Studio Profiler for detailed allocation analysis.

data.title: Memory Diagnostics Commands
data.code:
# Real-time GC metrics
dotnet-counters monitor --process-id <pid> System.Runtime

# Collect a memory dump
dotnet-dump collect -p <pid> -o crash.dmp

# Analyze dump
dotnet-dump analyze crash.dmp
> clrstack
> dumpheap -stat
> gcroot <address>

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Understand GC generations: Gen 0 for short-lived, Gen 2 for long-lived objects
Use Span<T> and stackalloc for zero-allocation operations on contiguous memory
Ref structs (like Span<T>) cannot escape the stack - use within methods only
ArrayPool<T> reduces allocations by reusing temporary buffers
Avoid boxing, string concatenation in loops, and unnecessary closures
Use StringBuilder instead of string concatenation in loops
Prefer manual loops over LINQ in performance-critical paths
Profile with dotnet-counters and dotnet-dump to identify memory issues
data.takeaway: Memory management in .NET is mostly automatic, but understanding how allocations and the GC work is essential for high-performance applications. Use stack allocation, memory pooling, and avoid common pitfalls to minimize GC pressure.
